🧠 Prompt Engineering is becoming much closer to Software Engineering than simply “asking AI the right question.”

One thing I’ve noticed while working with AI is that the quality of the response is often decided before the model even starts generating.

In real implementations, I don't want to rely on one clever prompt. The model needs clear context about what it is trying to accomplish, what information it can use, what it should avoid, and what a successful response should look like.

This becomes even more important with AI agents.

If an agent is investigating an incident, for example, the prompt alone isn't enough. It may need access to logs and metrics, tool definitions, environment context, permissions, previous findings, escalation rules, and a clear boundary around what it can and cannot change.

That’s why I see the evolution moving from:

Prompt Engineering → Context Engineering → Agent Engineering
The model is important, but the engineering around the model is what makes the output consistent enough to use in real workflows.

Another practice I find important is treating prompts like code: version them, test them against different scenarios, measure the results, and review changes before pushing them into production.

💡 A prompt that works once is a demo.

A prompt that works consistently across different inputs is engineering.

AI makes junior lawyers look better on paper, and that makes it far more difficult to tell whether they are learning. A recent field experiment gave 133 IP lawyers across 11 firms randomised access to an AI patent drafting tool over three months. Draft quality improved, and juniors benefited the most. The gains came from the lower end: fewer weak drafts, more average ones, and no increase in outstanding work. The tool raised the floor but left the ceiling unchanged. On a later redlining exercise without AI, seniors with seven or more years' experience who had used the tool outperformed their peers. Juniors showed no improvement on average, and their results diverged, with more very poor scores alongside more good ones.

The unaided markups explain the difference. Seniors restructured the draft to address its legal weaknesses and annotated each edit with the principle behind it. In interviews, they described treating the AI output as something to audit, which required them to articulate why each change was necessary. Many juniors identified serious defects without correcting them, leaving notes that read like instructions to an assistant who was not present. This habit was just as common among juniors who never had the tool in the study, and the researchers suggest it may stem from AI use outside the experiment. If so, it may already be taking root across the profession, regardless of any firm's formal AI policy.

In my view, juniors must learn to draft unaided first, and for longer than may seem efficient. The seniors benefited because they already knew what good work looks like. A junior without that foundation receives a competent draft and has no basis on which to question it. There is also a supervisory cost. Weak drafts have always shown a partner or general counsel which juniors need support. When the tool removes them, that indicator disappears, and a junior may appear ready for a year or two before the gap surfaces. The study is small and short, so its findings should not be overstated, but its lesson is clear: assess the lawyer's contribution separately from the tool's.

This has implications for how both law firms and in-house teams hire juniors. In private practice, associates have long learnt through billed volume. As AI absorbs that volume and clients grow less willing to pay for it, the training that came with the work will diminish unless firms build it back in. In-house teams are lean and typically hire juniors to relieve senior lawyers of volume work, which AI now does at lower cost. For both, the case for hiring a junior now rests on developing judgement, and the hiring process should test for it. Ask candidates to mark up a flawed contract without tools and explain every change, then set aside time for them to draft imperfectly and be corrected. If we hire juniors only to produce what the tool already produces, the profession will face a shortage of seniors within a few years, and no model can fill that role.

Mean time unemployed dropped to 24.9 weeks in July, from 25.5 in June. Payrolls grew by a modest 21,000 that same month, per the revised figures (the initial print showed a loss of 23,000). Read those two numbers together before you celebrate.

The headline version of this data sounds like progress. All three duration measures eased in July: mean down from 25.5 weeks, median from 11 to 10.5 weeks, long-term jobless (27-plus weeks) falling from 27.3% of the unemployed to 25.5%, or about 1.8 million people. On paper, the search is getting shorter.

The honest read: duration fell mostly because long-term jobless workers left the labor force entirely, not because a hiring surge absorbed them. A payroll gain of 21,000 doesn't come close to accounting for 166,000 fewer long-term unemployed. Labor force participation itself was down 0.7 percentage point since January. People stopped looking. A number drops when you remove the people for whom it's highest. That's arithmetic, not a hiring surge.

For someone weighing re-entry after a gap, this is the number that matters: not the shape of the headline, but what's behind it. The market isn't thawing. It's thinning at the edges.

What that means practically: the search is still roughly half a year of sustained effort. Not a reason to stay on the sidelines (waiting while the labor force contracts around you isn't a strategy), but a reason to be deliberate about how you run it. A months-long search conducted entirely by hand against a market this opaque tends to end in burnout or settling. Neither is re-entry on your terms.

Jobric runs the search in the background: ranked fits against your actual profile, not a feed you have to sift through manually, so re-entry doesn't become a second full-time job on top of whatever else you're managing.
